text: A yellow Citroën 2CV parked on the grass, with “007” on the door and fake bullet holes.
It is a copy of the car James Bond drives in For Your Eyes Only (1981). People walk past; another vintage car is in the background.
A small, slow car that became a film legend.
2cv-007.note: The 2CV was built from 1948 to 1990, a car designed to carry farmers and their eggs across a ploughed field.

art.commons: Usines Citroën, quai de Javel - btv1b532138417.jpg
art.caption: Agence Rol, Citroën works, Quai de Javel, 1929

scene: This park is named after André Citroën because his car factory stood here, at the quai de Javel, from 1919 until 1975.
The background photo shows the factory in 1929. The park opened on the same site in 1992.
2cv-007.approach: Last walk: down to the Seine and the Parc André-Citroën.

text: A large white stone monument behind a green railing.
Sculpted figures stand on steps on each side: soldiers and families. A standing figure in the middle stretches out its arm.
This is the war memorial of the 15th arrondissement, near its town hall.
monument-aux-morts-15e.note: Each 11 November, ceremonies are held at memorials like this one.

art.commons: Maréchal Ferdinand Foch saluant du bâton, à cheval, 14 juillet 1919.jpg
art.caption: Marshal Foch at the Victory Parade, 14 July 1919

scene: After the First World War, almost every town in France built a memorial. About 1.4 million French soldiers had died.
The background photo shows the Victory Parade on 14 July 1919, when the army marched through Paris after the war.
monument-aux-morts-15e.approach: We walk south-west into the 15th arrondissement, to the town hall.

text: A tall stone monument in the Luxembourg garden, surrounded by trees and grass.
At the top, a round bronze portrait of the writer Stendhal. Green streaks run down the stone below it: that is the bronze slowly oxidising in the rain.
The little sign in front explains that the medallion was made by Auguste Rodin, from a drawing by the sculptor David d'Angers.
stendhal-rodin.note: The Luxembourg garden has more than a hundred statues; this one is easy to walk past.

art.commons: Portrait de Stendhal en 1840, 88.23.jpg
art.caption: Portrait of Stendhal in 1840

scene: Stendhal (real name Henri Beyle, 1783–1842) wrote The Red and the Black in 1830, the story of an ambitious young man from the provinces trying to make it in society.
The background is a portrait of Stendhal from 1840. Rodin, the most famous sculptor of his time, made this medallion decades later.
stendhal-rodin.approach: We cross the river to the Left Bank and walk into the Jardin du Luxembourg.

text: A book on display in a shop window: Le Diable noir (“The Black Devil”) by Claude Ribbe.
The cover shows a portrait of a Black officer in a French general's uniform from the 1790s, with a sword and white trousers.
The book is about General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, a real person.
le-diable-noir.note: Paris has a monument to him, place du Général-Catroux in the 17th arrondissement.

art.commons: Thomas-Alexandre Dumas.jpg
art.caption: General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas

scene: Thomas-Alexandre Dumas was born in Saint-Domingue (today's Haiti) to a French nobleman and an enslaved woman. He became a general in the French Revolutionary army, at a time when that was almost unheard of.
His enemies called him “the Black Devil”. His son was the writer Alexandre Dumas, author of The Three Musketeers. The background is a portrait of the general.
le-diable-noir.approach: Back up in the street, a bookshop window.

text: A hand holds up the front page of Le Parisien.

The main headline: “Le moustique, ennemi public numéro 1” (“The mosquito, public enemy number one”), with a close-up of a tiger mosquito. On the side: a football story about Kylian Mbappé, a Toy Story 5 teaser, and a heatwave warning.
It is an ordinary day of news: insects, football, cinema and the weather.
le-parisien.note: Le Parisien was founded in 1944, at the Liberation of Paris, as Le Parisien libéré.

art.commons: Le Petit Journal - Apache.jpg
art.caption: Le Petit Journal, illustrated supplement, 'The Apache'

scene: Paris has always loved its daily papers. Around 1900, illustrated papers like Le Petit Journal sold about a million copies a day with dramatic colour covers.
The background is one of those covers. The style has changed, but the idea is the same: one big, scary image on the front to make you buy it.
le-parisien.approach: A café table on the way. Someone is reading the morning paper.

text: A carved stone inscription above a doorway, with “Galerie d'Apollon” written underneath.
It says, in French: “The Louvre Museum, founded on 16 September 1792 by decree of the Legislative Assembly, was opened on 10 August 1793 by decree of the National Convention.”
In other words, this is the museum's birth certificate, carved in stone right where visitors walk in.
louvre-galerie-apollon.note: The Galerie d'Apollon itself was decorated under Louis XIV; it now holds the French crown jewels.

art.commons: Hubert Robert - The Grande Galerie - WGA19594.jpg
art.caption: Hubert Robert, The Grand Gallery of the Louvre, c. 1795

scene: Before the Revolution the Louvre was a royal palace. In 1793 the revolutionaries opened it to everyone as a public museum, exactly one year after the fall of the monarchy.
The painter Hubert Robert worked on the new museum and painted the Grand Gallery many times. That is the painting behind this text.
louvre-galerie-apollon.approach: We cross to the Louvre and go inside, up to the Apollo Gallery.

text: Posters pasted over a grey metal shutter: the same red-and-white design repeated four times.
They say “Tu es communiste ? Rejoins-nous !” (“Are you a communist? Join us!”) with a black-and-white portrait of a bearded man and the logo “PCR”.
It is the same campaign as the sticker at the start of the walk, this time as big posters.
affiches-pcr.note: Pasting posters this way is usually illegal, so they are quickly covered or torn off.

art.commons: Manifestation du Front populaire au mur des Fédérés - btv1b90282283.jpg
art.caption: Popular Front demonstration at the Communards' Wall, 1936
art.credit: Agence de presse Meurisse. Agence photographique (commanditaire)

scene: Political posters have covered Paris walls for a long time. In 1936 the left-wing Popular Front won the elections and organised huge marches.
The background photo shows one of them, at the Communards' Wall in Père-Lachaise cemetery.
affiches-pcr.approach: Further on, a shop shutter covered in posters.

text: A red-and-white sticker on an old green door: “Tu es communiste ? Rejoins-nous ! Révolution” (“Are you a communist? Join us! Revolution”).
Someone has answered it by hand with a scribbled “Rebelle ?” on top. Part of the sticker has already been torn away.
It is a recruiting sticker for a small far-left group. The same campaign shows up again later on the walk, as full-size posters.
autocollant-revolution.note: Political stickers are the cheapest way to talk to the street: a few cents each, stuck where people walk past.

art.commons: Eugène Delacroix - La liberté guidant le peuple.jpg
art.caption: Eugène Delacroix, Liberty Leading the People, 1830

scene: “Revolution” is an old word on Paris walls. In July 1830 Parisians built barricades and forced King Charles X off the throne in three days.
Delacroix painted it the same year: Liberty Leading the People, now in the Louvre. The sticker uses the same word, almost 200 years later, on a much smaller scale.
autocollant-revolution.approach: From Point Zero we follow the quay. The first picture is on a door, at eye level.

text: A tall blind wall at the end of a building, against a bright blue sky.

A huge faded drawing in black and red lines covers it: big cartoon figures and little houses. Under it, someone has written by hand: “Vive la Commune” (“Long live the Commune”). A red tag sits at the bottom.
The slogan is small compared to the wall, but it is the part that tells you what the wall is about.
vive-la-commune.note: The background image is a barricade on rue de Castiglione, photographed during the Commune in 1871.

art.commons: La Commune 1871. Barricade rue de Castiglione, 1er arrondissement, Paris. PH20145.jpg
art.caption: Barricade on rue de Castiglione, Paris Commune, 1871
art.credit: Attribué à Braquehais, Auguste Bruno (Dieppe, 18–01–1823 - La Celle-Saint-Cloud, 1875), photographe

scene: The Paris Commune lasted from 18 March to 28 May 1871. After the war with Prussia, Parisians took over the city and ran it themselves for 72 days.
The army crushed it during the “Bloody Week”; thousands of people were killed. “Vive la Commune” is still written on Paris walls today, as a sign of protest and memory.
vive-la-commune.approach: Still along the river, a tall blank wall stands above the roofs.

text: A sheet of paper taped over graffiti: “C'est votre système qui est violent, pas les lycéen·nes !” (“It's your system that is violent, not the high-school students!”).
Below it, spray-painted in black: “NO WAR!” with stencils of rifles, and other tags.
The paper sign is neat and handwritten; the graffiti around it is messy. Two different ways of protesting on the same wall.
systeme-violent.note: In French protests, high-school students often march alongside university students and unions.

art.commons: Honoré Daumier, Rue Transnonain, le 15 avril 1834, 1834, NGA 6133.jpg
art.caption: Honoré Daumier, Rue Transnonain, 15 April 1834

scene: The slogan answers a common accusation: that young protesters are violent. It turns the question around and points at the state.
Artists made the same argument long ago. In 1834 Honoré Daumier drew Rue Transnonain, showing a family killed by soldiers in their own home in Paris. That is the background image.
systeme-violent.approach: A few streets further, a wall covered in tags.

text: A pale wall covered in marker: a big blue “ZERO” in the middle, and many smaller messages around it.
You can read “Free Palestine”, “Free Gaza”, “Mélenchon 2027”, “Nik la police” and “Qui pour nous protéger de la police ?” (“Who will protect us from the police?”).
Nobody planned this wall. Each person added a line, and together they make a kind of public conversation.
graffitis-zero.note: Mélenchon is a French left-wing politician; 2027 is the next presidential election.

art.commons: Umberto boccioni, rissa in galleria, 1910, 01.jpg
art.caption: Umberto Boccioni, Riot in the Galleria, 1910

scene: Graffiti walls show what is on people's minds right now: wars abroad, the next election, the police.
The background, Boccioni's Riot in the Galleria (1910), shows a crowd in movement: many voices at once, like this wall.
graffitis-zero.approach: On the way out of the garden, a wall full of writing.

text: A black shop sign on a dark façade: “Big Black Cook”, in big white letters, with a smaller pink line underneath.
It is the sign of a small restaurant at 5 rue Tiquetonne, a narrow street full of places to eat.
The picture is just the sign: simple, bold, and easy to spot from the end of the street.
big-black-cook.note: This is one of the six photos we could place exactly on the map.

art.commons: Léon Augustin Lhermitte - Les Halles - musée des Beaux-Arts de la ville de Paris.jpg
art.caption: Léon Lhermitte, Les Halles, c. 1895

scene: Rue Tiquetonne is right next to Les Halles, which for centuries was the city's huge food market. Writer Émile Zola called it “the belly of Paris”.
The background painting by Léon Lhermitte shows the market around 1895. The market moved out of Paris in 1969, but the neighbourhood is still all about food.
big-black-cook.approach: We head north into the 2nd arrondissement, towards Les Halles and rue Tiquetonne.

text: The front of a small Italian restaurant. Above the door, a blue banner: “Forza Napoli”, the chant of the Naples football club.
The windows are covered in photos of players and the club's blue colours. Inside, people are eating; outside, a woman is on her phone next to a scooter.
A little piece of Naples in a Paris street.
forza-napoli.note: Napoli fans are known for their devotion to Diego Maradona, who played for the club in the 1980s.

art.commons: Béraud - Le boulevard des Capucines, le soir, devant le Café Napolitain, Vers 1880.jpg
art.caption: Jean Béraud, In Front of the Café Napolitain, c. 1880

scene: Italian immigrants have lived in Paris since the 19th century, and they brought their cafés and food with them.
The background painting by Jean Béraud shows the Café Napolitain on the boulevards around 1880, already a famous meeting place.
forza-napoli.approach: Further on, a small restaurant with blue flags.

text: A stall with a handwritten sign: “Handmade drawings 25€”.
One drawing, in black ink, is captioned “Kill the past, embrace the future”. A man points a pistol away while kissing a woman; another woman sits at a table with a glass and a cake, ignoring them.
It is a funny, dramatic scene, sold by the artist on the street for the price of a lunch.
dessins-faits-main.note: Funny detail: we have just left the Louvre, the museum the Futurists wanted to burn.

art.commons: The City Rises by Umberto Boccioni 1910.jpg
art.caption: Umberto Boccioni, The City Rises, 1910

scene: “Kill the past” is almost word for word what the Italian Futurists said. Their manifesto was published on the front page of Le Figaro, in Paris, in 1909: burn the museums, love speed and machines.
The background is a Futurist painting by Umberto Boccioni, The City Rises (1910).
dessins-faits-main.approach: Back outside, near the river, someone is selling drawings.

text: A bus-shelter poster for Burger King, in a JCDecaux frame.
It shows an “Ice Burger”: ice cream between two bun halves, with chocolate on top. The slogan: “Un ovni parmi les desserts” (“A UFO among desserts”).
A burger that is actually a dessert: the ad is built to make you look twice.
abribus-burger-king.note: JCDecaux invented the advertising-funded bus shelter in 1964, in Lyon.

art.commons: Apéritif Mugnier affiche, Jules Chéret 90.jpg
art.caption: Jules Chéret, poster for Apéritif Mugnier

scene: Street posters became an art in Paris in the 1890s. Jules Chéret printed bright, colourful posters for drinks, theatres and cafés; people collected them.
The background is one of Chéret's posters, for an apéritif. Same idea as the Burger King ad: bright colours and one product.
abribus-burger-king.approach: We wait at a bus stop for a moment.

text: A big advertising poster in a métro station, on the classic white tiles.

It is for Deblock, a finance app: “Le compte courant pour vos euros, bitcoins et stablecoins” (“The current account for your euros, bitcoins and stablecoins”). The bank card says “Own your money”, in the style of a video game logo.
A very modern ad, in a station design that has barely changed in a hundred years.
deblock-metro.note: The first métro line opened in 1900, for the Universal Exhibition.

art.commons: Robert Delaunay, Hommage à Blériot, 1914.jpg
art.caption: Robert Delaunay, Homage to Blériot, 1914

scene: The métro opened in 1900 and quickly became a place for posters. Each new technology has promised to change everyday life: then electricity and aeroplanes, now crypto.
The background is Robert Delaunay's Homage to Blériot (1914), painted for the pilot who first flew across the Channel.
deblock-metro.approach: We go down into the métro. White tiles, a long corridor.

text: A busy street corner. The pedestrian light is green, and people are crossing.
Around them: tall cream-coloured buildings with iron balconies, a scooter, cafés at street level.
Nothing special happens in this picture, and that is the point: it is everyday Paris.
feu-vert.note: Haussmann's works destroyed a large part of medieval Paris to build the city we know today.

art.commons: Gustave Caillebotte - Paris Street; Rainy Day - Google Art Project.jpg
art.caption: Gustave Caillebotte, Paris Street; Rainy Day, 1877

scene: These buildings are typical of Baron Haussmann, who rebuilt Paris between 1853 and 1870 with wide avenues and matching façades.
Gustave Caillebotte painted people crossing one of these new streets in 1877: Paris Street; Rainy Day, the background image. It looks almost like this photo, 150 years earlier.
feu-vert.approach: We cross a big Paris crossroads.

parc-de-l-etrange.place: A gate, on an October evening
text: A black banner on a fence in front of tall trees: “Le Parc de l'Étrange”, in red letters (“The Park of the Strange”).
The smaller line says: “L'événement immersif d'Halloween” (“The immersive Halloween event”).
A haunted park for one month a year, set up like a theme park.
parc-de-l-etrange.note: The Catacombs are open to visitors and are one of the most visited places in Paris.

art.commons: Nadar - Catacombes de Paris - NPS 74.jpg
art.caption: Nadar, Catacombs of Paris, 1861–1862

scene: Paris has always liked to scare itself. Under the city lie the Catacombs, old quarries filled with the bones of millions of Parisians.
The background is one of the first photos taken underground, by Nadar in 1861, using electric light.
parc-de-l-etrange.approach: In the evening we reach a park gate with a black banner.

text: A purple concert poster: “Gospel Dream — chants authentiques de l'église afro-américaine” (“authentic songs of the African-American church”).
It shows a choir in purple robes inside a church. The concert is at the Église Saint-Louis-d'Antin, on Friday 1 May at 8:30 pm.
We placed it near that church, since the poster probably hangs in the area.
gospel-dream.note: Saint-Louis-d'Antin was built in the 1780s as the chapel of a convent.

art.commons: Joséphine Baker - photo Waléry.jpg
art.caption: Waléry, Josephine Baker, c. 1926

scene: African-American music has a long history in Paris. In the 1920s jazz arrived, and Josephine Baker became a star of the Paris stage. She is in the background photo.
Today, gospel concerts in Paris churches are a way to hear that tradition live.
gospel-dream.approach: We walk north towards Saint-Lazare, into the 9th arrondissement.

text: A street sign: “Rue du Palais”, with a small coat of arms, on the corner of a stone building.
Below it, graffiti in pencil-thin letters: “Macron castration”, and a tag.
The coat of arms and the orange building in the back look like Grenoble rather than Paris.
rue-du-palais.note: We are not sure where this photo was taken. The original file with its GPS would tell us.

art.commons: Journée des Tuiles (Alexandre Debelle), Musée de la Révolution française - Vizille.jpg
art.caption: Alexandre Debelle, The Day of the Tiles, 1889

scene: If this is Grenoble, rue du Palais is named after the old Parliament building. In June 1788, people there threw roof tiles at the king's soldiers: the “Day of the Tiles”.
Many historians see it as one of the first sparks of the French Revolution. That event is in the background painting.
rue-du-palais.approach: We leave Paris for the last three pictures.

une-solution-revolution.place: Beyond the walls — a pink façade
text: A pink building on a quiet street, with a parked car and someone sitting by the door.
On the wall, in black spray paint: “Une solution : révolution” (“One solution: revolution”).
Same word as at the very start of the walk, now on a completely different wall.
une-solution-revolution.note: This photo does not seem to have been taken in Paris.

art.commons: Prise de la Bastille clean.jpg
art.caption: Jean-Pierre Houël, The Storming of the Bastille, 1789

scene: “Revolution” in France always points back to 1789 and the storming of the Bastille, shown in the background painting.
Graffiti like this uses that history as a shortcut: one word, and everybody knows what it means.

nike-la-police.place: Beyond the walls — a pink wall
text: A pink wall with black graffiti: “Nike la police”.
It is a play on words: “Nique la police” is a rude slogan against the police (“Screw the police”), here spelled like the sportswear brand Nike.
Brand names and protest mixed together, which is how a lot of street language works today.
nike-la-police.note: This photo also does not seem to have been taken in Paris.

art.commons: Affiches Charles Verneau. "La Rue " - affiche - Steinlen 96 - btv1b9011731v.jpg
art.caption: Théophile Alexandre Steinlen, The Street, 1896

scene: Théophile Steinlen drew the streets of Paris in the 1890s: workers, children, cats, posters. His big poster “The Street” is the background.
The street has always been where people show what they think, with drawings, posters, or a can of spray paint.

start.title: Point Zero, square in front of Notre-Dame
